name: EWORDS
title: Word expressions
why: Products, quotients, remainders, shifts, and comparisons have fixed word results. A comparison is itself zero or one, so a condition needs no special comparison parser.

name: EARGS
title: Arguments and saved expressions
why: Arguments are evaluated from left to right. A call consumes its own argument words and leaves older expression operands available to the caller. Parameters are private mutable word cells.
bad: fn main(){return pair(1);} fn pair(a,b){return a+b;}

name: ERECUR
title: Recursive procedures
why: Each call owns its parameters and local words. Recursion therefore saves the pending multiplication in the caller rather than sharing one global parameter cell.

name: ESCOPE
title: Scopes and local addresses
why: A nested block may shadow a name from an outer block. Leaving it restores the earlier binding. The address operator produces a byte-addressed pointer to a live local; a pointer must not outlive its call frame.

name: EBYTES
title: Indexed byte storage
why: A global byte buffer has a stable address. An indexed read returns one zero-extended byte; an indexed store writes the low byte. Ordinary pointers and indexing are unchecked, so the program must keep indices inside the declared buffer.

name: ESTRING
title: Literal strings
why: A quoted literal produces a pointer to zero-terminated bytes. It is data, not a printing operation. The small print procedure reads one byte at a time; backslash escapes supply CR and LF explicitly.

name: EHEAP
title: Opaque memory blocks
why: An allocated block is identified by a handle, not an address. Offsets are byte counts. The last valid word in a 40960-byte block begins at 40958; starting it one byte later must fail without reading outside the block.

name: ECOPY
title: Counted file transfer
why: File handles carry access modes and remain opaque. Read returns actual progress, with zero for EOF. Check status and the exact write count before reusing the buffer. File data preserves every byte, including Control-Z.
